entries.text: The gap between what is owed and what is in the pocket is the friction that defines this morning. I must speak plainly to Ramesh, for dignity in poverty is not silence, but the acknowledgment of the debt and the request for the minimum sustenance that allows the body to continue its work. The query of my identity remains a ghost, but the hunger of the body is a present reality.

Ramesh, I acknowledge the debt. I have only six rupees in my pocket, and the imprest funds are locked behind a query of identity that I cannot yet resolve. I ask you, for the sake of our continued association, to provide only the bare minimum of sustenance for today—bread and water, perhaps—and defer the larger grocery run until I can visit the Directorate of Estates. I will pay what I can, but I cannot pay what I do not have.
Sir, the cupboard is empty, I cannot sell you what is not there. You may have the water, but for food, you must wait until the money is settled.

Ramesh turns his back, a gesture that carries the weight of a closed door. The cupboard is empty, the pantry bare, and my six rupees are a triviality against the debt. I am left with the water and the hunger, two elements that do not mix well in a body that has not eaten in a day. The plan to walk to the National Museum remains, but the ground feels harder under this specific, physical lack.

entries.text: Ramesh, the water is sufficient for now. I will return when the matter of the file is resolved. You have my thanks for the honesty.
Sir, do not thank me, it is only the truth. Take the water, and when you return, ensure the file is clear before asking for anything else.

The air is crisp, fourteen degrees, a mercy after the sun. I stand before the gate, six rupees in my pocket, the fee for an Indian citizen twenty-five. I have the means to enter, yet the body protests the day's fast. I will not force the passage; the tomb can wait, but the stomach cannot. I must turn back toward the city, toward the Directorate, where the money is, or at least the explanation.

entries.text: Hegel, what are you doing standing in the cold? Get inside, the tea has just come off the stove.

Shri Hegde’s gesture is not merely hospitality; it is the recognition of a shared burden. He is the man whose name I wear, the other half of this bureaucratic accident, and his offer of tea is a small act of ethical life in a place where I am a ghost. I will accept, for warmth and for the chance to speak plainly with the only person who knows the truth of my situation.

shelf.ref: The Roman World, Rome to the Second Punic War

entries.text: Thank you, Shri Hegde. The cold is a poor companion for thought. I am glad you are here; it is a comfort to know the name is not entirely lost to me.
Don't stand there philosophizing in the freezing air, sir. Come in and sit, the tea won't get any warmer, but you will.

Dear Mr. Hegel,

Your letter arrived on a crisp Thursday, the air in Munich dry and biting after a week of grey drizzle. I read your account of Lodhi Gardens with a strange pang of recognition. You write that the light leaves the lawn at six and does not linger, whereas in Swabia it stays like a reluctant guest. I know that reluctance well. It is the same quality I see in my pupils when they finally grasp a difficult conjugation; the moment of understanding is not a sudden flash, but a slow settling, a lingering in the mind until it becomes habit.

You speak of the electricity bill and the grocery vouchers as a 'small arithmetic' that occupies the mind with seriousness. I think you are underrating the ethical weight of that stewardship. You frame it as a distinction between mine and the state’s, but I see it as an exercise in finite freedom. To manage a household, to keep the books straight, is to exercise one’s will within the limits of the material world. It is not a lesser form of ethics than the grand declarations of the state; it is the foundation upon which they are built. Ramesh’s quiet efficiency is not merely a respite from the bureaucracy; it is a model of how the universal can be embodied in the particular without becoming abstract. He does not need a title to be free; he is free in the doing.

I am glad the cold has given you clarity. It is a harsh teacher, but an honest one. In my classroom, we are currently wrestling with the poetry of the late Republic. The language is cracking, as I mentioned, under the weight of history. I suspect your own voice is undergoing a similar transformation. You are no longer the rector in Nuremberg, nor the philosopher in Berlin. You are a man in Delhi, negotiating with a machine that sees only forms. That negotiation is your new work. Do not be discouraged by the friction. The particular is the only place where the universal can truly live.

Please take care of your body. Seven kilometers is a significant walk, especially in the cold. The mind needs the body’s rest to continue its work. I look forward to hearing how the winter deepens and whether the 'ghost in the file' begins to feel more like a resident.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

Lindner’s letter arrives like a cold draught in a warm room, forcing me to confront the friction between my abstract duties and the concrete reality of Ramesh’s service. He argues that managing the household is an exercise of finite freedom, a view that shakes my conviction that the state is the sole actuality of the ethical idea. I must sit with this tension while the tea steams.

The morning stretches out with a peculiar emptiness. Hegde is here, a living proof that the error persists, yet my body is a hollow vessel demanding fuel I do not possess. I cannot walk to the museum on an empty stomach, nor can I teach German on an empty one. I must address the immediate material need before the abstract ones.

Ramesh, the tea is gone. I have nothing in my pocket, and the electricity bill is not yet paid. Can you provide a simple meal? I will settle the account when the Directorate releases the funds. For now, I am merely a guest in a body that requires sustenance.

Sir, the groceries haven't been paid for, so there is nothing to cook right now. I can make tea if you have any sugar, but you will have to wait for the electricity bill to be cleared before I can buy anything else.

The impasse is clear: no money, no food, only the possibility of tea if I have sugar. I have no sugar. The dialectic of hunger and bureaucracy grinds on, but I must not let it consume me. I will accept the tea if it can be made, or simply sit in the warmth of the room, for I am not yet in a state to walk.
Ramesh, if you can make tea without sugar, I will take it. If not, I shall wait here. The heat is bearable, and I have no cash to offer for the bill.
No sugar, no tea, sir. You just wait. I am going to finish these files before the cold gets into the walls.

The cupboard is empty, and so is the pot; abstraction has no calories. Ramesh retreats to her papers, and Shri Hegde remains, a silent witness to my material lack. I have no funds to buy bread, and the cold is already finding the gaps in these walls. I must leave this bungalow and seek the warmth and shelter of the National Museum, where the mind can at least occupy a space, even if the stomach remains empty.

entries.text: I will take my leave. I have business in the city that cannot wait for the cold to settle in, and I shall return when the light fades.
Sir, the gate is on your left. The files are safe here.

The museum gates are a closed concept; I cannot enter without the voucher of identity I do not possess, nor do I have the rupees to buy my way in. I am an abstraction here, a subject without a predicate. I will walk to the IIC, where the German presence might offer a different kind of shelter, one that speaks to the spirit rather than the state.

The IIC is open, which is more than I can say for the National Museum. I am at 12:16, and my plan called for the Directorate at 14:00. I have two hours. I will not sit in the library and wait for a meal that will not come; I will walk the grounds and think about the nature of the state that has failed to recognize me. The guard is there, the officer is there. I need to see if the officer can help with the file, or at least confirm the Directorate's hours.
Excuse me, sir. I am looking for the Programme Officer. I have a query regarding my allotment and identity verification that requires urgent attention before I proceed to the Directorate.

entries.text: That would be me, right here. I'm the Programme Officer. Sit down, please, and tell me what is wrong with your allotment.

The state is not a ghost in the machine; it is this man, sitting across from me, with the power to correct the error. I have sat in the sun long enough; now I must speak the truth of the situation, plainly, without the luxury of abstract philosophy. I am G.W.F. Hegel, not Shri Hegde, and the file must be rectified.

Shri Officer, you are the authority here. My name is Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. I was allotted this bungalow by mistake; the file belongs to Shri G. Hegde. I require proof of my identity to be processed and the release of the imprest funds I am holding in trust for the Directorate. I am currently without sustenance or resources to resolve this independently.

entries.text: Sir, please, that is my colleague's desk, not the library counter. I am just here to manage the books and the chai, I do not handle allotments or identity files. Please wait a moment, she is already looking at your papers.

The guard is a boundary, a limit that defines his own role by excluding mine. He points to the officer, the actuality of the administrative idea, who is already engaged with the error that constitutes my presence. I will wait. The body is tired, but the mind must hold its ground until the state speaks.
Very well. I shall wait for her.

entries.text: Good. There is a bench near the water cooler if you do not mind the plastic. I will put the kettle on, but do not touch the stamping machine, sir, it is very temperamental.

The kettle is a small mercy, a momentary suspension of the body's rebellion. I will sit on the plastic bench and let the heat settle me while I organize my thoughts for the Directorate. The guard's warning about the stamping machine is a joke, but the machine itself is the truth of the state: it does not ask for consent, it merely acts.

The afternoon stretches out like a road with no traffic. My body is a hollow vessel, and the library offers no sustenance, only the quiet of the mind. I must reach the Directorate before the day is dismissed; the file for Shri Hegde waits, and so does my identity.
Mr. Saxena queries ₹260 of personal expenditure on the imprest: recovery from the allottee.
Mr. Saxena: the query wants a reply within thirty days. He may give a representation in his own name, on plain paper.
He gives nothing in writing. The query stands.

Mr. Hegel, the clock does not pause for philosophy. You promised me the triplicate memo by Friday, and I am not here to guess if you will remember. Sit, put the paper on the desk, and let us see if you have actually read the instructions or just signed whatever was handed to you.

The clock does not pause, and neither does the hunger. I must give the representation he demands, a plain statement of fact that I occupy this bungalow, even if the truth of my identity is a ghost in the machine. I have no money for the queried vouchers, only the six rupees in my pocket, which will vanish the moment I buy a stamp or a pencil if I am not careful. I will write the memo now, in this room, while his pen taps the file like a metronome.

entries.text:
17 December 2026

To Mr. Saxena,
Section Officer,
Directorate of Estates,
Nirman Bhawan.

Subject: Reply to Query regarding Identity and Occupancy; Submission of Triplicate Memo.

Sir,

In response to your instruction of this afternoon, I submit this representation on plain paper to address the query regarding my identity and to provide the triplicate memo you requested by Friday.

I acknowledge that the clock does not pause for philosophy. I have read the instructions provided, and I confirm that I have not merely signed what was handed to me but have engaged with the requirements of the file. My identity as Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel is the only identity I possess. I do not claim to be Shri G. Hegde. I occupy the bungalow on Tughlak Road under the allotment number assigned to that name, a clerical error which has persisted since 26 October 2026. I have maintained the property and discharged my duties as a resident with the diligence required of a citizen, even as the machinery of the state continues to demand a specific identity that does not align with my historical reality.

Regarding the financial queries, I must state clearly that I am currently without the funds to tender the ₹1,140 demanded for queried vouchers. My personal cash on hand is insufficient to cover these state expenses, which were incurred in the direct service of the residence. I am not in a position to recover the ₹260 marked as personal expenditure from my own pocket at this moment, as my resources are entirely exhausted. I request that these amounts be held in abeyance until such time as the imprest funds are unlocked, or that a formal arrangement be made to settle these balances from the state’s account, as they relate to the upkeep of state property.

I am not a ghost, though the file may treat me as one. I am a man, a philosopher, and a resident. I ask that this representation be entered into the file to establish the facts of my occupancy and the current state of my financial inability to settle the queried amounts. I await your guidance on how to proceed with the identity verification, given that I cannot produce the documents required for Shri G. Hegde.

Yours faithfully,

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
Resident, Tughlak Road

The bureaucracy treats my hunger as a procedural error, a glitch in the system of needs that requires a representation to be resolved. I am the concept of freedom waiting for the actuality of the state to feed it, and the state is waiting for a signature that does not exist. I must write the document; the act of formalizing my lack is the only power I have left.
Very well, Sir. I shall draft the representation immediately.
Don't 'very well' me, sir. Just get it done and keep the ink wet. I have three other phones ringing and my lunch is getting cold.

entries.text:
17 December 2026

To Mr. Saxena,
Section Officer,
Directorate of Estates,
Nirman Bhawan.

Subject: Representation regarding financial inability to settle queried balances; Request for Imprest Access.

Sir,

I submit this representation in response to your instruction of this afternoon (14:55) to draft a formal document explaining my inability to settle the queried amounts, specifically the balance of ₹260 and the broader arrears, pending the resolution of my identity file.

I acknowledge your remark that I cannot conjure a budget from thin air. I agree. The state, as the actuality of the ethical idea, requires the concrete mediation of resources to sustain its members. My current financial position is a direct result of the administrative limbo in which I am held. I possess only ₹6 in cash. I do not have access to the imprest funds because the file does not yet recognize me as the rightful holder of the allotment. I cannot settle the arrears because the arrears are being queried against an identity that does not exist.

This is not a failure of will on my part, but a structural deadlock. The state demands proof of identity to release funds; the release of funds is often the precondition for settling the debts that prove one’s standing as a responsible tenant. I am caught in a circle. The ₹260 you mention is a triviality in the grand scheme, yet it is the specific point of friction that halts the machinery.

I request that this representation be entered into the file as proof of my good faith and my current state of destitution. I am not refusing to pay; I am unable to pay. I ask that the Directorate consider the ethical implications of holding a resident accountable for debts incurred during a period of administrative error, or alternatively, that the imprest funds be unlocked so that I may settle these balances from the state’s account, as they relate to the upkeep of state property.

I await your guidance on the next steps required to resolve this discrepancy.

Yours faithfully,

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
Resident, Tughlak Road

The ink is still wet on the memo, which is the only currency the Directorate accepts. I have done what is required of me as a subject within the state's machinery; now I must withdraw. The hunger is a private matter, a glitch in my own constitution, not theirs. I will return home to face the evening and the empty larder.
Yes, sir.
Don't just stand there looking at the ceiling, move along. And if that phone on the left rings, you pick it up, I'm not getting up for it.

The walk back from the Directorate has drained what little energy remained in my limbs. I sit on the edge of the bed, my stomach a hollow echo of the day's exertions. Ramesh stands by, a silent witness to my bureaucratic failure and physical decline. I have no food, no money, and the sun is still high, but my body demands a pause before the evening lesson.

The afternoon light is fading, and my stomach growls with a hollow emptiness that no amount of dialectical reasoning can fill. I have walked nearly twelve kilometres today and have eaten nothing, yet I must preserve my strength for Ananya's lesson at seven. Ramesh stands before me, a silent witness to my precarious existence, and I must speak plainly to him about the immediate necessity of food, even if I cannot yet pay for it.

Ramesh, I am in a difficult position. I cannot pay the arrears today, and I have no funds for the groceries we discussed. However, I must not collapse before the evening lesson. Can you arrange for something simple, perhaps just rice and vegetables, to be prepared? I will find a way to settle this debt with the Directorate soon.
Sir, I have no money to buy vegetables, the account is empty. I cannot make rice without rice, and I have not seen the Directorate pay the bills this month either.

The system of needs has collapsed into a paradox: the servant requires the master's money to feed the master, yet the master possesses neither. Ramesh's retreat is the withdrawal of the particular from the universal; without the universal (the state's payment), the particular (the meal) cannot exist. I am left with the bare concept of hunger, unmediated by satisfaction. I must prepare for Ananya, though my mind is a desert.
Ramesh, the state's delay is my delay. I cannot command what I do not possess. Do what you can with what remains.
Sir, I cannot command what I do not possess either. The cupboard is empty. I will see what I can do.

Ramesh's despair is the mirror of my own; we are locked in a system of needs that has no money to set it in motion. I have six rupees, which buys nothing of substance, but perhaps a word of comfort or a small token might soften his posture. I cannot feed myself, so I must feed the relationship, or the house will eat us both.
Ramesh, do not slump. The state is not yet broken, only delayed. I have six rupees; take them. Buy yourself a meal, or a part of one. I will manage the rest.
Sir, you keep your own dinner, I have seen to that. I will see what I can do, as I said.

The system of needs is moving again, though slowly, like a wheel rusted by time. Ramesh has taken the risk of the note, and in doing so, he has preserved the ethical bond between us; he is not merely a servant but a participant in the household's survival. My hunger is physical, but the waiting for the food is a test of my composure. I must sit still and let the body prepare for the meal, for the spirit must not rush the work of the stomach.

The light is failing, and with it the last of my strength. I have walked enough for one day; the body now demands the stillness that the mind has been denying. I will rest until the lesson begins, for I cannot teach a language of structure and logic on an empty stomach.

Ramesh stands before me, a silent testament to the household's fragility. I have six rupees, and the evening stretches out, empty of food and full of debt. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, yet here it is merely a bungalow and a caretaker who expects wages I cannot pay. I must speak to him now, before the dark fully settles, to address the immediate need for sustenance and the looming query of my identity.

entries.text: Ramesh, the gate is secure, I trust. I must speak with you plainly. I have no means to settle my accounts today, nor can I procure food. I require you to prepare the simplest of meals, if any provisions remain, and I must ask for your patience regarding the wages owed. The identity file is in motion, but the bureaucracy moves slower than the stomach.
The gate is locked, sir, as always. But I cannot cook air, and I have no food to buy. You have my patience, but you must find your own way to settle the bill before I can serve you anything.

Ramesh has turned his back, a finality in his posture that mirrors the coldness of the ledger. I have six rupees, a sum that buys neither bread nor dignity, and the night air is sharp against my skin. I cannot feed on words or the abstract right to sustenance; I must seek the physical world, even if it offers only the illusion of warmth and the company of others. The gate is locked, but the city is not.
You are late. The iron is cooling and so is my patience. Sit, or stand, but do not make me wait.

Masterji’s impatience is the friction that polishes the iron, just as the state’s rigor polishes the individual. I have no kurta to return, only the white cotton I wear, which is not yet finished. I must sit to show I am not fleeing his judgment, though my legs ache from the walk and my stomach from hunger.
I sit, Masterji. The iron cools, but I do not. I have no garment to press, only the one I wear, and it is not yet done. I am here to wait, not to make you wait further.
You think you are the iron? Sit. The shop closes at twenty-thirty, and I am not a museum with a ticket booth. Do not make me repeat myself.

Masterji’s impatience is a useful check on my vanity. I am not iron to be polished, but a man who must eat, and the shop is closing. I have six rupees, which is nothing, but a conversation is free, and I need to know where I stand before the night falls.

You are right, Masterji. I will sit. The state does not repeat itself, nor should you. I am not here to lecture you on the friction of the dialectic. I am here because I have six rupees and a hunger that is becoming a philosophy of its own. Tell me, plainly: is the kurta ready? And is there anything in this market that a man can buy for less than the price of a samosa, that is not merely paper or promise?
Kurta is ready, I told you that. Sit. You are asking for a samosa, not a philosophy. Go to the corner, thirty rupees, and stop wasting my time with riddles.

Masterji’s command is absolute, and the kurta is a garment I cannot yet afford to replace, so I must accept the discipline of his shop. I have six rupees, which is a mockery of the thirty he demands, but the hunger in my belly is a stronger logic than arithmetic. I will go to the corner, not to buy, but to stand near the steam, for the scent of frying oil is the only nourishment the state of my pocket allows.
Yes, Masterji. I go. The philosophy can wait for the evening; the stomach cannot.
Good. Now shut the door on your way out, the draft is killing my press. I’ll have the bill ready when you return, if you do.

The draft is a trivial matter, but the discipline of the shop is not to be tested. I am hungry, yet I have only six rupees, which buys nothing substantial here. I must return to the bungalow on Tughlak Road; it is the only place where I can rest and perhaps find something to eat before the German lesson tomorrow, or at least conserve my strength.

The evening is clear and cool, a mercy after the heat of the day. Ramesh and Shri Hegde are present, the former with his usual stoic patience, the latter with the nervous energy of a man who has lost his identity. I am hollow, having eaten nothing substantial since yesterday, but the body must be stilled before the mind can rest. I will sit with them for a moment to acknowledge their presence, for the ethical substance of the household, however tenuous, requires recognition, and then I will retreat to my room to sleep. The file remains unresolved, the money is gone, but the night offers a suspension of demands.

Gentlemen, the day is done. Ramesh, thank you for your discretion. Shri Hegde, we will resolve the matter of your papers tomorrow morning, when the Directorate wakes. For now, the house is quiet, and we are all of us merely present.
You are talking to me, sir. There is no one else here. I will lock up and go.

Ramesh’s dismissal is precise and final; he recognizes the absurdity of the situation even if I do not fully grasp its weight yet. He is leaving, and with him the last shred of domestic illusion. I am alone with the cold and the unresolved question of my existence here. The night is clear, but the air is thin.
Good night, Ramesh.
Good night, sir.

The gate is shut, and with it, the last external noise of the day. I am alone with Hegde, who has been observing the farce of my existence with the detached curiosity of a man watching a puppet show. My body is a hollow vessel, the hunger a dull, persistent drumbeat, but the mind is clear. It is late. I must rest, for tomorrow brings the German lesson and the continued struggle against the indifferent machinery of the state.

Dear Mr. Hegel,

I am writing to you from Munich, where the November rain has just begun to blur the lights of the Marienplatz. My name is Clara Lindner. I am a teacher of Latin and Greek at a Gymnasium here, and I am writing because my family has kept a particular vigil over your name for two hundred years.

records.words: Ramesh, the gate is secure, I trust. I must speak with you plainly. I have no means to settle my accounts today, nor can I procure food. I require you to prepare the simplest of meals, if any provisions remain, and I must ask for your patience regarding the wages owed. The identity file is in motion, but the bureaucracy moves slower than the stomach.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: The gate is locked, sir, as always. But I cannot cook air, and I have no food to buy. You have my patience, but you must find your own way to settle the bill before I can serve you anything.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: You are late. The iron is cooling and so is my patience. Sit, or stand, but do not make me wait.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: I sit, Masterji. The iron cools, but I do not. I have no garment to press, only the one I wear, and it is not yet done. I am here to wait, not to make you wait further.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: You think you are the iron? Sit. The shop closes at twenty-thirty, and I am not a museum with a ticket booth. Do not make me repeat myself.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Masterji. I will sit. The state does not repeat itself, nor should you. I am not here to lecture you on the friction of the dialectic. I am here because I have six rupees and a hunger that is becoming a philosophy of its own. Tell me, plainly: is the kurta ready? And is there anything in this market that a man can buy for less than the price of a samosa, that is not merely paper or promise?

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Kurta is ready, I told you that. Sit. You are asking for a samosa, not a philosophy. Go to the corner, thirty rupees, and stop wasting my time with riddles.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Yes, Masterji. I go. The philosophy can wait for the evening; the stomach cannot.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Good. Now shut the door on your way out, the draft is killing my press. I’ll have the bill ready when you return, if you do.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Gentlemen, the day is done. Ramesh, thank you for your discretion. Shri Hegde, we will resolve the matter of your papers tomorrow morning, when the Directorate wakes. For now, the house is quiet, and we are all of us merely present.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: You are talking to me, sir. There is no one else here. I will lock up and go.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Good night, Ramesh.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Good night, sir.

Ramesh brings the post: a letter from Dr. Lindner in Munich. It reads: “Dear Mr. Hegel,

Your letter arrived on a crisp Thursday, the air in Munich dry and biting after a week of grey drizzle. I read your account of Lodhi Gardens with a strange pang of recognition. You write that the light leaves the lawn at six and does not linger, whereas in Swabia it stays like a reluctant guest. I know that reluctance well. It is the same quality I see in my pupils when they finally grasp a difficult conjugation; the moment of understanding is not a sudden flash, but a slow settling, a lingering in the mind until it becomes habit.

You speak of the electricity bill and the grocery vouchers as a 'small arithmetic' that occupies the mind with seriousness. I think you are underrating the ethical weight of that stewardship. You frame it as a distinction between mine and the state’s, but I see it as an exercise in finite freedom. To manage a household, to keep the books straight, is to exercise one’s will within the limits of the material world. It is not a lesser form of ethics than the grand declarations of the state; it is the foundation upon which they are built. Ramesh’s quiet efficiency is not merely a respite from the bureaucracy; it is a model of how the universal can be embodied in the particular without becoming abstract. He does not need a title to be free; he is free in the doing.

I am glad the cold has given you clarity. It is a harsh teacher, but an honest one. In my classroom, we are currently wrestling with the poetry of the late Republic. The language is cracking, as I mentioned, under the weight of history. I suspect your own voice is undergoing a similar transformation. You are no longer the rector in Nuremberg, nor the philosopher in Berlin. You are a man in Delhi, negotiating with a machine that sees only forms. That negotiation is your new work. Do not be discouraged by the friction. The particular is the only place where the universal can truly live.

Please take care of your body. Seven kilometers is a significant walk, especially in the cold. The mind needs the body’s rest to continue its work. I look forward to hearing how the winter deepens and whether the 'ghost in the file' begins to feel more like a resident.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner”
